hops.title: The shovel for the chicken shed
hops.text: In one of Michael Gazzaniga's split-brain tests, a patient's speaking left hemisphere was shown a chicken claw while his right hemisphere was shown a snow scene. Asked to point to a matching card, his right hand, run by the left hemisphere, chose a chicken, and his left hand chose a snow shovel. Then he was asked why. His left hemisphere had never seen the snow, but it did not say so. It answered at once: "Oh, that's simple. The chicken claw goes with the chicken and you need a shovel to clean out the chicken shed."

sources.citation: Marinsek, N., Turner, B. O., Gazzaniga, M., & Miller, M. B. (2014). Divergent hemispheric reasoning strategies: reducing uncertainty versus resolving inconsistency. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 8, 839.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A person seen from behind facing a screen with a chicken claw and a snow scene, pointing with each hand to a hen card and a snow shovel card.
image.caption: Missing the snow scene, the speaking hemisphere explained the shovel with a chicken shed instead.

hops.title: Whistled Turkish and the right hemisphere
hops.text: In Kuşköy, a village in the mountains of northeast Turkey, people switch from spoken Turkish to whistles to talk across distances of up to several kilometers. Whistled Turkish keeps the words and grammar but carries them in pitch and melody, sounds the right hemisphere is specialized to encode. Onur Güntürkün and colleagues played 31 whistlers competing syllables through headphones, one in each ear. For spoken syllables, people reported far more from the right ear, the usual sign of left-hemisphere speech processing. For whistled syllables, the two ears came out about even. The same language, carried by a different sound, lost its usual asymmetry.

sources.citation: Güntürkün, O., Güntürkün, M., & Hahn, C. (2015). Whistled Turkish alters language asymmetries. Current Biology, 25(16), R706-R708.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two distant figures seen from behind on opposite green slopes of a misty valley, one cupping hands to whistle across.
image.caption: Spoken syllables favored the right ear; whistled ones showed no clear advantage for either ear.

hops.afterHeading: How precise is the map? Lesions and living brains
hops.title: What the brain uses to read computer code
hops.text: Python is called a programming language and is full of English words like if and for, so it was a fair guess that reading it would use the brain's language network. In 2020, Anna Ivanova, Evelina Fedorenko and colleagues tested that with fMRI in 24 Python programmers and 19 users of ScratchJr, a graphical language. They first found each person's language regions with a sentences-versus-nonwords contrast, then gave code problems and matched problems written as English sentences. The language regions responded strongly to the sentences, weakly to Python and not reliably to ScratchJr. Code mostly engaged bilateral regions used for math and logic.

sources.citation: Ivanova, A. A., Srikant, S., Sueoka, Y., Kean, H. H., Dhamala, R., O'Reilly, U.-M., Bers, M. U., & Fedorenko, E. (2020). Comprehension of computer code relies primarily on domain-general executive brain regions. eLife, 9, e58906.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An open laptop showing abstract colored shapes beside a puzzle cube and a mug, with a closed novel set aside.
image.caption: Code engages the brain's math-and-logic regions, while its language regions respond weakly or not at all.
